item.title: South Korea’s First Lady: Institutional Ambiguity and Hanbok Diplomacy
item.body:
In February 2026, South Korea’s First Lady Kim Hea-kyung was officially appointed as Honorary Hanbok Ambassador by the Hanbok Globalization Foundation¹. This topic is noteworthy because of the presidential spouse’s high public exposure, which amplifies the political sensitivity of her move². With unresolved debates over official administrative oversight, it is a pressing challenge for the government to define the proper scope for the First Lady’s activity. Thus, this commentary analyses how Cultural Diplomacy, specifically Hanbok Diplomacy, serves to define and legitimate her public function within the boundaries of non-political representation.

Unlike the President, who has an independent electoral mandate, the First Lady is not elected to the office and does not hold institutional power. Furthermore, her role is not well-defined legally³. So, on what definition and standard does the public evaluate the person in this position? For instance, the United States First Lady operates within an institutionalised framework codified under the White House Personnel Authorization Act of 1978, which legally recognised her as a “de facto officer” with a stable budget and staff assigned to her office, the East Wing⁴. Or in France, following the public backlash over presidential spouse privilege in 2017, the government issued a “Transparency Charter” (Charte de transparence) that clearly defined the role, operational limits, and staff sizes of the President’s spouse⁵. However, South Korea lacks a clear definition of her “powers, duties, roles, or responsibilities in the Constitution or other laws”⁶. At the same time, there have been recurring domestic controversies over successive First Ladies in South Korea: (1) abolition or reinstatement of the “Second Secretariat” (제2부속실), which is the First Lady’s office⁷, (2) shadow power⁸, and (3) lavish lifestyle⁹. All of which point to the institutional vacuum of this position in South Korea.

Therefore, through Kim Hea-kyung’s appointment as Hanbok Ambassador, we can see how a South Korean First Lady can establish a specific public role through promoting Hanbok on the global stage. In June 2025, she wore Hanbok to attend the G7 summit¹⁰; later in October 2025, she also wore Hanbok to the APEC summit¹¹; then in February 2026, she was appointed as the Honorary Hanbok Ambassador. These events demonstrate that even before her appointment, she had already been showcasing Korea’s traditional attire at international events. Therefore, the appointment of Hanbok Ambassador can be seen as a recognition and formalisation of her role in promoting Hanbok. Like the “Transparency Charter” issued by the French Government, Kim Hea-kyung’s appointment is a pragmatic institutional workaround. **Through Hanbok promotion, Kim represents Korean cultural heritage and participates in international cultural exchange without being directly involved in policymaking or exercising political authority.**

In conclusion, the appointment of Kim Hea-kyung as Hanbok Ambassador seems to be a workable solution for the structural deficit. That way, she could be active in cultural diplomacy with less chance of being criticized for political overstepping because the role defined her as the presidential spouse for promoting cultural heritage on the global stage. However, the issue of her role ambiguity remains domestically, on whether the Korean media and public will actually recognize this cultural shield or continue to criticise her wardrobe spending. This remains an unresolved debate that might shape the future of the First Lady’s office.

item.summary: This commentary analyses how cultural diplomacy, specifically Hanbok diplomacy, serves to define and legitimate the public function of South Korea's First Lady within the boundaries of non-political representation.
